text: Cassini ran out of fuel. It was going to be steered into Saturn’s atmosphere. NASA wanted to keep the spacecraft from drifting into space. Earth microbes could be on the probe. Saturn’s moons have water, and some might hold it under ice. Enceladus sprays water from its south pole. If Cassini crashed there, it could plant Earth life. Crashing into Saturn’s upper atmosphere burned up the probe. The planet did the work. Saturn is huge. Its atmosphere is thick enough to destroy a small spacecraft. That’s the whole point. It wasn’t a planned “suicide” for drama; the fuel was simply gone.

Your stationary leg hurts because it is doing more than you think. When you ride, one leg pushes, the other leg holds the board in line. That holding leg keeps the ankle and the hip under constant tension. The muscles stay tight for a long stretch. Tight muscles get tired and send pain signals to the brain. A lot of riders lean on the front foot or lock the back foot against the board. That locks the joint and makes the surrounding muscles work harder. The pressure sits on the ankle bone or the sole of the foot. If you keep the leg still, blood flow slows and local stiffness builds. The pain can show up in the calf, shin, thigh, or hip, depending on where you brace. I'd stop treating the stationary leg as an idle part. Your stance decides which muscles take the load. If your front foot points sideways, the ankle twists slightly. If your back foot stays flat and rigid, the knee takes extra strain. Try moving that leg a little more. Shift your weight. Keep the ankle loose and the knee bent a bit. Your leg hurts because you are holding a moving board with a still limb. That's a stiff stance. It feels fine for a few minutes, then the muscles start screaming. Check where the board meets your foot. A worn deck edge can press into the top of the foot or the ankle. Your foot may arch away from that pressure. The calf tightens to stop the board from tilting. If you ride with a fixed back foot, the hip abductors and adductors work quietly in the background. They don't burn the way pushing does, but they accumulate load. That quiet load is what becomes ache later. Let the foot roll on the deck. Keep the knee under the hip. Don't let the leg go wooden. A small bend and a small shift make the pain go away faster.

Yes, the name is historical, not a claim that most of them live in Africa or were born there. "Afro-American" grew out of the civil rights era. Black leaders in the 1960s and 1970s wanted a name that connected American Black people to their African roots. The term came up in political speeches, community groups, and newspaper writing. It was a political identity, not a passport record.

Most African American families did not sail to America from Africa personally. Enslaved people were taken from West and Central Africa, and their descendants lived in the US for many generations. That does not erase the connection. The name points back to where the ancestors came from, the way "German-American" points back to Germany, even if the family has lived in the US for two hundred years.

Calling the group "Afro-American" was also a way to push back on old labels. People wanted a name with some pride in it. That is a blunt take, but I think it makes sense. The term stuck in dictionaries, schoolbooks, and government forms, so now you see it everywhere.

Syrians get their weapons from captured army depots and local dealers. Governments and neighbors supply them. A militia takes a warehouse full of rifles. A trader brings crates over a border road. A faction receives a container from a sponsor country. They still get them because the fighting has not stopped. One side still holds more guns, and each group wants the advantage. Some buy from online dealers. Paying in gold is a dumb way, but gold coins still work very often. A new shipment means a new front or a new commander. It signals a fresh push for ground.

It feels weird that people act like every drug is a bad thing. Some medicines save lives, and some recreational drugs have a long human history. But when you ask for a drug that gives intense pleasure with zero adverse effects, you're asking the brain to enjoy a very strong reward without changing itself. That's the hard part.

Opioids like heroin bind opioid receptors, and cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake. Both make the reward signal jump. The brain reads that jump as too much. It responds by turning the signal down. You need more to get the same high. That drop in response is tolerance. If you stop, the brain is left running lower than before. That shows up as withdrawal. The pleasure and the bad side effects come from the same push.

A drug could be gentler. It might have fewer withdrawal symptoms. But if it still delivers intense euphoria, it still forces adaptation. The reward circuitry does not know the difference between a useful medicine and a party drug. It balances the signal. That balancing is where tolerance and withdrawal come from. A high with zero adverse effects would have to make the brain happy without making it adjust. I don't see how that works for a strong drug.

There is also the practical side. Alcohol is everywhere, but it still causes blackouts and liver damage. Nicotine is milder in some ways, but it still creates cravings. Caffeine is taken daily by most people. It can cause jitters and sleep trouble. So the word 'drug' does not mean poison. It means a substance that changes brain chemistry. The question is how hard it pushes that chemistry.

I think the confusion comes from mixing two ideas. People say all drugs are bad because the famous bad ones get all the attention. The real issue is the strength of the reward signal and how much the brain adapts. A drug with intense euphoria will be hard on the brain. I'd take a milder drug with a gentler rise if I could, but I don't know of a powerful one that leaves no trace. Most strong highs do leave a mark on the body. The brain pays for every strong reward. I'd rather have a drug that lifts you without wrecking you. That's why I don't expect a painless party drug anytime soon. That's the part most forum answers miss.

Hi,
That shopping pain is real. When you walk for hours, your legs and feet carry you the whole time. You carry bags and keep pace with your wife. Your muscles work nonstop. They ache. Your feet swell, too. A short break helps your legs reset. Your head gets a different pain when you are tired and hungry. That is not a normal headache. It is your body running out of fuel. Drink water and eat during the trip. If the pain stays after you rest, see a doctor. I'd just bring snacks and water, not a fancy plan.
Cheers,
Sam

Hi,
Your brother ran a quick trick on you. You said silk five times in a row. That repeated sound stayed in your head. Silk and milk share the -ilk ending. When he asked what cows drink, your mouth reached for the rhyming word before your mind reached for the correct answer. Cows do drink water. Your answer was a slip from the repeated sound. The word silk had just worn a path to milk. I think that is why milk came out. The trick works on most people, and you were caught by it. He wanted to see you stumble. He didn't mean to confuse you about animals. He was testing how fast a rhyming word can take over. You probably heard yourself say milk and felt surprised. That is the point of the test. Your attention was stuck on the repeated word.

Cheers,
Alex

Hi Sam,

You didn't list the questions, but here's the part that usually bites people. Start with the budget before you look at kitchens. Lenders cap the loan, and that cap decides the street you can afford. Check the mortgage rate before you fall in love with a kitchen. Rates move, and a half point can change the monthly payment.

When you visit a house, look at the roof, drains, windows and outside walls. Those are the expensive fixes. A pretty house with a cracked foundation will cost more than it looks. Get a survey before you pay the deposit. The surveyor will name the defects, and then you can renegotiate or walk away.

If you are buying with a partner, agree on who pays for what before you sign. Money fights start long before the wedding. Put the deal in writing, even if it's just a one-page note.

For the paperwork, chase your lawyer. They should send the contracts for you to read. The small clauses hide the big costs.

I'd just ask the seller what they know about the house before the lawyer starts.

Cheers,
Alex

Hi Sam,

A 3-in-1 bodywash/shampoo/conditioner is one formula intended to clean skin and wash hair in the same shower. A separate body wash cleans skin. A shampoo cleans hair. A conditioner leaves softening agents on the hair. The 3-in-1 has to work on two very different materials, skin and hair. Its surfactants are usually milder than a strong body wash, and it adds moisturizers and conditioning agents. A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner only deals with hair. It combines shampooing and conditioning in one bottle, but it does not replace a body wash. It covers body and hair with one mild formula. You use one product in the shower for body and hair. The formula cannot be as targeted as separate products. If your hair needs real conditioning, or your skin needs more cleaning power, separate products may work better. I wouldn't rely on the 3-in-1 for daily hair care if your hair is damaged or very oily. I'd only use it for light, everyday needs. It is fine for travel or a quick shower, but it is not a full replacement for separate body wash and hair products. Your results depend on hair type and skin type.

Cheers,
Alex

Hi Sam,

GPS stations are the main tool for this. Surveyors install receivers on bedrock at many points across a continent. Each receiver gets signals from orbiting GPS satellites. The receiver solves its three-dimensional position by timing those signals, and the same stations are observed again months or years later. The change in position gives velocity, usually reported in millimeters per year. The satellite signals let the receiver compute position to millimeter accuracy after corrections for atmosphere and clock errors.

The math compares one station to another on the same landmass or across two plates. If the stations drift toward or away from each other, that drift is the plate motion. Satellites also provide reference frames, and agencies like NASA and USGS publish these velocities for tectonic plates. These numbers are then fitted to a global plate motion model.

Older evidence from fossils and rock formations helps set the long-term picture, but GPS gives the direct modern measurement. The rates are tiny, a few centimeters per year. One station has to be measured over a long baseline to separate real motion from noise. They also track the slow widening of the Red Sea and the spreading ridge under Iceland.

Cheers,
Alex

Inbreeding does not directly lower IQ. It changes the odds of inheriting certain gene combinations.

Every person carries several rare harmful gene variants. If two unrelated parents both carry a variant, their child usually inherits one copy, and the variant stays hidden. Related parents are more likely to carry the same variant, because they may have inherited it from the same ancestor. A child can then receive two copies, one from each parent, and the variant can affect brain development, learning, or mental health. For example, if two cousins both carry the same variant, the child's risk of inheriting two copies is higher than with unrelated parents.

The closer the parents are related, the higher the chance that hidden variants become active. The result is not a fixed IQ score. Some inbred children are average or high, while others have cognitive difficulties. It is a probability, not a sentence.

Getting hit in the arm often hurts less because the arm is padded with muscle and fat, and it does not hold the heart, lungs or spine. A blow to the forearm or upper arm lands on soft tissue, and the pain is usually local. The torso and head contain vital organs and dense nerve networks, so injuries there carry a higher risk and often feel more severe. Pain also depends on where nerves are concentrated. The arm has fewer pain-sensitive structures than the abdomen, chest or face.

Adrenaline and shock can make an arm wound feel smaller than it is. If a bone or joint is involved, the pain can be much worse. For a new colleague, the short version is: arm injuries are common and often seem manageable because the arm is built to move and absorb impact, not because all arm injuries are minor.

Carbon monoxide starves your blood of oxygen. It comes from incomplete combustion, like a car engine or a gas stove left open. It is colorless and odorless, and you cannot smell it. Once it enters the lungs, it moves into the blood. There, it binds to hemoglobin, the protein that normally carries oxygen. Carbon monoxide holds on much more tightly than oxygen. That makes it hard for the blood to deliver oxygen to your heart and brain. Your body keeps asking for more air, but the gas does not let oxygen attach to the hemoglobin. The shortage reaches the brain first. You get a headache, then you lose consciousness.

A car idling in a closed garage can fill the room fast. A gas water heater or candle in a small bathroom can do the same. The room stays quiet, and the gas has no smell. You feel fine until your head starts to hurt. Then the confusion comes. People often mistake it for tiredness. The longer you stay, the more hemoglobin gets blocked. If you feel a headache near a gas appliance, leave the room. Open a window. Let the air move. You can protect yourself by keeping vents open and using a carbon monoxide detector. The alarm tells you before your body does. A detector costs less than a hospital bill.

Carbon dioxide builds up when a room has little fresh air. Your lungs remove it, but the room keeps making more. In a sealed space, the level rises. At around 0.5%, you may feel drowsy. At around 15%, you can pass out. That is not the same as carbon monoxide poisoning. Carbon monoxide does this much faster and at lower levels. What matters is the grip on hemoglobin.

When a plane hits rough terrain, a hard landing, or a collision, the body keeps moving even after the aircraft stops. The seatbelt holds your hips, but your head and torso still lurch. The brace position limits that lurch. You lower your head to the headrest or to your knees. You cross your arms and grip the back of the seat in front of you. Your feet go flat on the floor. Your knees bend, and your arms take some of the force that would otherwise hit your neck and spine. The position keeps your head from striking the seatback. It reduces the chance of a neck injury or a broken wrist. It also gives your body a defined path for the impact.

A hard landing can be genuinely brutal, but the brace position makes that brutality more manageable. It does not make the impact completely painless. It just gives your body a way to absorb the hit. Think of it as turning a loose load into a braced frame. The crew will shout 'brace, brace'. You take that position as soon as they do. Keep your fingers away from the seatback so your hands do not get trapped.

There are old trades, but a well-known brand needs mass recognition. Before industry, firms were small, regional, and family-run, so names rarely spread beyond a town. Early records were scarce, and many ledgers were lost in wars or floods. Industry changed the setup: factories, railroads, and the telegraph let goods and names travel fast. Mass advertising, standardization, and national markets then turned local shops into household names. A business can be centuries old without being famous. That combination of a long run, repeat customers, and a recognizable name is rare in the pre-industrial record.

The dealership's low APR is a trap. I side with the bank, because the advertised rate hides the real bill. The dealer quotes 2.9% on a $25,000 loan for 60 months. That number looks better than my bank's 3.4%. But the dealer wants to bundle a gap insurance policy, a service contract, and pre-paid maintenance into the loan. In my example, those add-ons and doc fees add $1,200 to the balance. The bank charges a $100 fee and leaves the loan clean.

At 2.9%, the dealer loan payment is about $448 a month. At 3.4%, the bank payment is about $453 a month. The lower dealer rate saves five dollars monthly. Over sixty months, that is only $300. The dealer's $1,200 in fees wipes out the saving and then some. I'd just take the bank.

Dealerships can quote a lower rate because they often receive a subsidy from the manufacturer or the finance company. The low rate is a sales tool. They pair it with products you did not ask for. The car price may already include fees that the bank would not charge. You can negotiate the add-ons, but the paperwork is written to make you accept them. A service contract and gap insurance can each run into the hundreds or thousands. The loan term also matters. A dealer may offer a shorter term at the low rate, which raises the monthly payment and changes the total interest.

Dealers also split the deal price into cash and finance portions. The low rate applies to the financed portion, while the cash portion can carry its own fees. The finance office earns its commission on those products. That is why the sheet says one rate while the invoice says another. Many dealers get rate caps from the manufacturer. They advertise the capped rate, then fill the gap with products. The finance office makes money on the gap. The lower APR does not cover the full cost of the car. You pay for the products whether you want them or not. That is why the sheet and the invoice do not match. Check both numbers before you sign. Ask for the payoff total, then call the bank. And compare the two written numbers.

Keep the two sheets side by side. Circle every fee that is not part of the car price. The bank quote should show the payoff total. Write it down.

I'm for states deciding for themselves. If a state wants to sell marijuana in shops, let it. I can buy a bag at a dispensary in Colorado, then ride my car into Wyoming and feel unsure. Two dozen states and the District of Columbia have adult-use laws, but the federal government still calls it a Schedule I drug. A state tax office in Oregon collects taxes on legal sales, while the IRS can still look at the same income. I'd rather have a single federal rule, but that rule should let states keep their shops open. It is odd that a state can sell what the federal government still treats as a hard drug. I want the law to follow the shelf: if the state license is on the wall, the plant in the jar is legal there. People pay taxes, and they can't always know which rules apply here.

I think your body is a living battery. It makes electricity the same way a battery works: ions move, and that movement is the spark. In your nerves, a thin membrane separates fluid inside the cell from fluid outside. A signal arrives, small gates open, sodium rushes in, potassium leaves, and the cell's voltage flips. That flip travels down the nerve like a wave. Your heart has its own little conductor, a patch of tissue that sets the beat, and your muscles fire the same way. The tingle in a numb hand is the wiring briefly jammed. That is your own electricity doing its job.

Musicians sample older songs by lifting a short piece of a record and working it into a new track. I like it when the borrowed sound keeps its old flavor. The producer finds a record on vinyl or a digital file. They listen for a drum break or a vocal phrase. That is the raw material. They pull out a few seconds, then trim the edges. The clip needs to fit the tempo. They stretch, slow, speed up, or pitch shift it. A 1970s funk loop can become the drum pattern for a rap song. A 1980s vocal can become a melodic hook. The producer puts it under new beats and writes around it.

Clearing rights is the practical part. A sample touches two copyrights. The song composition belongs to the songwriter. The master recording belongs to the record label. The producer needs permission from both. Labels often charge a fee. Some allow a short snippet for free. That limit is not a magic safe zone. Courts can still look at how recognizable the snippet is. I think the free snippet rule is a dumb design. It gives people false comfort. A recognizable two-second piano hit can still lead to a claim.

Many musicians avoid the paperwork. They use a sample library. A library gives you loops and one-shots with a simple license. That license says what you can do with the sound. It also says how you must credit the original artist. Some libraries charge a flat fee. You can build a track without tracking down a 1975 label office. For a serious release, the producer sends a written request to the rights holders. The request names the song and the seconds used. It also asks how the track will be sold. The label replies with a fee or a flat license. If the label says no, the producer swaps the clip for something else.

I prefer samples that leave room for the original. If the old song is buried under too many layers, the listener cannot tell where it came from. A good sample is a conversation. The new beat speaks first. The old fragment answers. That is what makes sampling different from covering a song. You can hear the year it came from. I keep a folder of clips I would like to use, and I tag each one by source and seconds. I check the waveform before I send a clip to a label. That check saves a week of back-and-forth.

When my head hurts, I stop and look at the place that aches. It is usually at the temples or behind one eye. That spot feels tight, as if a band is squeezing it. I take a slow breath and let my jaw and shoulders drop away from my ears. The pressure in that spot eases a little.

I have learned to treat a headache like a small warning from the body. Dehydration or poor sleep can build up the tightness. I drink water and step outside for air. I give my eyes a break from the screen. Most of the time, the pain moves from a dull throb to a mild ache, then disappears.

Some days it stays. I take a pain reliever and lie down in a dim room. I check the clock and my water bottle. The room is quiet. The headache tells me something needs attention.

I can't even tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We got there Sunday at 7:20 p.m. We picked this place specifically because of a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel. We figured it'd be easy. We wrote our names into their completely useless digital waitlist. At 8:23 p.m. we were told to come back to pay. We did. We stood around until 8:40 p.m., when staff casually said we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15 p.m. It was just a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait stretches that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn't completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m. No line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than I'd expected to pay at a steakhouse.

I was pretty disappointed that steak wasn't offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else. Those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I really didn't want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn't try any.

Overall, I'd call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it actually offers. If you're curious, it's definitely worth trying once, especially if there's no line or wait. But if the line is long, I'd probably reconsider going.

Four stars, and I'm keeping it. The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so “example” becomes “eexample” and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it still stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life—well, the under-21 version—so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too—the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a “rip-off” way exactly, just... if you’ve seen Cirque du Soleil, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many “wow” moments stacked on each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing—more must be better—so they crammed everything in.

If you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal—$99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. A few friends liked it. If you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave completely overwhelmed.

The shirts never came. About two years ago, we called Rockmount Ranch Wear and ordered two shirts for my father. The sales representative wrote the delivery address down wrong. Her handwritten 7 looked like a 1. We wanted 5407, but the shirts went to 5401. The people at 5401 took the package to the local UPS store to send it back. The package vanished and no one heard anything else. Several weeks passed before we found out. While the dispute was going on, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount would not refund the first two. The owner took over that part. He admitted the shipment had gone to the wrong address, but he said no refund until the shirts were returned. He said we were partly at fault because we had not been friendly enough to the people at 5401, four doors away. We put in a credit-card dispute over the original charge. In the end, we got a credit.
